case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Bay Outfitters (KBO) is a public limited company in the outdoor clothing retail and e-commerce sector, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2007 by Rhea Kestrel, the chain sells waterproof jackets and hiking gear through high-street stores and its own website across six countries, and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. KBO plans to invest $900,000 in a new automated distribution warehouse, financed by a $600,000 ten-year bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $324,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $30, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. KBO faces two problems: absenteeism is rising and picking errors in the warehouse have increased.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report, Q3 2025: KBO's distribution centre packed 17,500 orders last quarter with a picking error rate of 3.2%, down from 5.0% last year. Customer complaints fell from 61 to 34 per month. Average delivery time is 5.2 days. Market research of 520 shoppers found 63% would pay up to $2.00 more for responsibly sourced materials, and 49% compare delivery speeds before ordering. Records show 16 of 48 staff still need on-the-job training on the new barcode scanners; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $950 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Kestrel Bay Outfitters as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.8%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 4.9% from $13.80 to $14.48 an hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale textile and freight input costs have risen 11.2% year on year, while consumer spending on outdoor clothing grew 3.1%.

questions.question_text: KBO plans to fund part of its warehouse expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for KBO of using a share issue to finance the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises $300,000 of equity that never has to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike the $600,000 bank loan. With fixed costs of $324,000 a year and an 11.2% rise in textile and freight costs, avoiding debt service protects KBO's cash flow and leaves more of the $30 selling price available to absorb cost increases.

Point 2: Equity does not require collateral, so the $900,000 automated distribution warehouse is not at risk of repossession if sales disappoint. It also strengthens the balance sheet ahead of future borrowing, which matters for a public limited company answerable to shareholders. The 63% of 520 surveyed shoppers who would pay $2.00 more for responsible materials give a growth opportunity that can be pursued without the lender conditions attached to a bank loan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KBO's costs, expansion finance and market evidence.

questions.question_text: KBO is launching a new responsibly sourced outdoor jacket range. Consider a national television campaign, search-engine advertising, or outdoor influencer marketing. Which should KBO choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV advert could quickly build awareness of KBO's waterproof jackets across all six countries and support its high-street stores. However, airtime and production are very costly for a business already funding a $900,000 warehouse, and the mass audience includes many non-buyers, so spend would be poorly targeted.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search reaches buyers at the moment they look for hiking gear, is measurable and can be capped to a budget, protecting cash flow alongside the $600,000 loan. Its limitation is that it captures only existing demand and does little to build the responsible-sourcing message that 63% of 520 shoppers value, while clicks in competitive outdoor categories are costly.

Outdoor influencer marketing: Walking and climbing influencers can demonstrate the jackets in real conditions and explain responsible sourcing to an audience that already buys outdoor clothing, matching the 49% of shoppers who compare delivery speeds and care about purchase details. Credibility is high and spend is targeted, although results depend on the influencer's reputation and may build slowly.

Recommendation: KBO should choose outdoor influencer marketing with a small search budget. It demonstrates product performance, reaches the specific outdoor segment and supports the $2.00 responsible-sourcing premium. Television is rejected as too expensive and untargeted; search alone is rejected because it cannot create the brand pull needed for a new jacket range.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of promotional methods with minimal reference to KBO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two methods applied to KBO's retail and online business.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three methods with a justified recommendation that rejects television and explains the limits of search advertising.

questions.question_text: KBO's absenteeism is rising and warehouse picking errors have increased. Explain two benefits for KBO of using autocratic leadership to improve performance in its distribution centre.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Rhea Kestrel set clear, uniform picking procedures for the 48 staff, which directly addresses the rise in picking errors from 5.0% to 3.2% shown in the report and brings consistency across shifts. In a hierarchical structure, quick decisions can be imposed without delay, protecting the 5.2-day delivery promise.

Point 2: Firm direction can tighten attendance expectations and reduce the absenteeism that disrupts the 17,500 orders packed each quarter. With a $600,000 loan to service, management control over routines and the $950 training budget ensures the 16 staff needing scanner training are prioritised, safeguarding the $900,000 warehouse investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of autocratic leadership identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KBO's errors, absenteeism, structure and training.

questions.question_text: KBO must train 16 warehouse staff to use the new barcode scanners. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should KBO choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the packing line is specific to KBO's own scanners and processes, costs no fees, and keeps the 16 staff productive on the 17,500 orders handled each quarter. It directly targets the picking error rate that has fallen from 5.0% to 3.2%. Drawbacks are that the trainer's productivity drops, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate for staff.

Off-the-job training: College courses at $950 per employee cost $15,200 for the 16 staff, a small share of the $900,000 investment. They provide structured skills and a recognised certificate, useful for a public limited company with shareholders. However, staff are absent from the warehouse, worsening the 5.2-day delivery time in the short term, and generic content may not match KBO's scanners, so on-site follow-up would still be required.

Decision: KBO should choose on-the-job training first, with short college sessions later for supervisors. It is cheaper, scanner-specific and avoids losing output while absenteeism is already rising and errors still need attention. Full off-the-job training is rejected because $15,200 and the loss of 16 staff from the line would disrupt deliveries during the expansion, and autocratic management can enforce consistent on-site practice immediately.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KBO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in KBO's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption, error reduction and scanner relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KBO's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $324,000 ÷ ($30 − $18) = $324,000 ÷ $12 = 27,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 27,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $30 − $18 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KBO's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare break-even output of 27,000 units with output of 70,000 units to show a margin of safety of 43,000 units, confirming the warehouse can be used fully without immediate losses.
2. Use the $2.00 premium that 63% of shoppers would accept to model contribution rising from $12.00 toward $14.00, helping decide whether responsible sourcing is worthwhile.
3. Set sales targets that cover $324,000 fixed costs and $600,000 loan repayments, checking the 70,000-unit plan can service debt.
4. Monitor unit cost ($324,000 ÷ 70,000 + $18 = $22.63) each quarter to benchmark the new distribution centre and detect waste behind the 3.2% picking error rate.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 27,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 70,000-unit output; modelling the $2.00 responsible-sourcing premium; loan-service volume targets; and unit-cost benchmarking at $22.63 to monitor picking errors.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in each of (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KBO's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has KBO's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 2.03 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.87 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.85 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 + $94,000 + $62,000 = $366,000; 2025 current assets = $186,000 + $118,000 + $48,000 = $352,000. For 2024, $366,000 ÷ $180,000 = 2.03; for 2025, $352,000 ÷ $196,000 = 1.80. Excluding stock: 2024 ($366,000 − $210,000) ÷ $180,000 = $156,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.87; 2025 ($352,000 − $186,000) ÷ $196,000 = $166,000 ÷ $196,000 = 0.85.

Evaluation: Liquidity has deteriorated on both measures. Coverage of short-term obligations fell from 2.03 to 1.80 because current assets dropped by $14,000 while liabilities rose from $180,000 to $196,000. The stock-excluding measure also slipped, from 0.87 to 0.85, showing KBO is no more able to meet debts without selling inventory, a concern while it services a $600,000 loan and commits $900,000 to a warehouse. Cash fell from $62,000 to $48,000 and inventories from $210,000 to $186,000; receivables rose to $118,000, tying up cash. The buffer at 1.80 is still adequate, so the position is not critical.

Conclusion: KBO's financial position has not improved. Both measures fell and the stock-excluding measure also weakened, so the decline is not explained by inventory alone. KBO should tighten credit control over the higher receivables and rebuild cash before drawing further on debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion that the position has not improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KBO of switching to responsibly sourced materials for its outdoor clothing.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Responsibly sourced materials match the 63% of 520 shoppers who would pay up to $2.00 more, protecting the $12.00 contribution per unit as textile and freight costs rise 11.2%. It supports the brand behind the $900,000 warehouse and may raise the 70,000-unit sales plan.

Disadvantage: Certified materials usually cost more than standard fabric, raising the $18 variable cost per unit unless the full $2.00 premium is accepted. Any supplier delay would lengthen the 5.2-day delivery time and risk complaints, while the 3.2% picking error rate still needs attention at the new distribution centre.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KBO's survey data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.8%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in textile and freight costs will affect KBO. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.8%): If KBO's $600,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.8% of $600,000 = $4,800 a year (0.008 × $600,000). This is small relative to fixed costs of $324,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the direct effect is zero. Higher rates could dampen outdoor-clothing spending and raise future borrowing costs, but the risk is manageable and can be hedged by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (4.9%, to $14.48 an hour): With a workforce of 48, higher hourly pay raises KBO's wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual wages, so an annual total cannot be invented; the defensible benchmark is productivity of 70,000 ÷ 48 = 1,458.3 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it falls, the $12.00 contribution per unit is eroded.

Textile and freight inflation (11.2%): The $18 variable cost per unit is exposed, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an illustrative bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.2%, that adds 11.2% × $18 = $2.02 per unit, about $141,000 a year at 70,000 units. The $2.00 premium 63% of shoppers accept can offset part of this.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in textile and freight costs has the greatest impact. It applies to every unit sold, directly threatens the $12.00 contribution that supports the $900,000 expansion, and is only partly recovered through pricing; the interest effect is modest and the wage effect turns on unstated hours.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KBO.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on KBO's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in KBO's context with a justified greatest-impact judgement that avoids invented figures.
